paragraphs.context: a large pleasant meadow with a pond of clear water in it
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horse remembers his first home: a field with a pond, trees, a gate, a house, and a brook.
paragraphs.simple: The first place I can remember well was a big, nice field of grass with a pond of clear water in it. Some shady trees leaned over the pond, and rushes and water-lilies grew at the deep end. On one side, over the hedge, we looked into a plowed field. On the other side, we looked over a gate at our master’s house, which stood by the road. At the top of the field there was a small group of fir trees. At the bottom there was a running brook with a steep bank hanging over it.

paragraphs.context: to the doctor’s, to the farrier’s, and no doubt to Squire Gordon’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: People ride off to bring help. The farrier looks at the black horse. It has a broken leg, and the horse is shot.
paragraphs.simple: People now rode off in every direction: to the doctor’s, to the farrier’s, and without doubt to Squire Gordon’s, to let him know about his son. Mr. Bond, the farrier, came to look at the black horse that lay groaning on the grass. He felt him all over and shook his head. One of the horse’s legs was broken. Then someone ran to our master’s house and came back with a gun. Soon there was a loud bang and a terrible cry, and then everything was still. The black horse moved no more.
paragraphs.main: Men ride off to tell people. The farrier finds that the black horse has a broken leg. A gun is brought, there is a loud bang, and the black horse moves no more.

paragraphs.context: Everyone may not know what breaking in is, therefore I will describe it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Beauty explains breaking in. A horse must learn to wear a saddle, a bridle and harness, and to obey. He must keep calm and do what his master wants.
paragraphs.simple: Not everyone may know what breaking in is, so I will tell you. It means teaching a horse to wear a saddle and bridle and to carry a man, a woman or a child on his back. The horse must go just the way they want, and go quietly. He must also learn to wear a collar, a crupper and a breeching, and to stand still while they are put on. Then a cart or a chaise is fixed behind him, so that he cannot walk or trot without pulling it after him. He must go fast or slow, just as his driver wants. He must never jump with fear at what he sees. He must not speak to other horses, or bite, or kick, or have any wish of his own. He must always do what his master wants, even if he is very tired or hungry. The worst thing is that once his harness is on, he cannot jump for joy or lie down when he is tired. So you see, breaking in is a big thing.
paragraphs.main: Black Beauty explains what breaking in is. A horse must learn to wear a saddle, a bridle and a harness, to pull a cart, and to always do what his master wants.

paragraphs.context: Squire Gordon’s park skirted the village of Birtwick
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horse tells us about the park at Birtwick and the stable where he is taken: it is large, airy and has four good stalls.
paragraphs.simple: Squire Gordon’s park went along the edge of the village of Birtwick. You came in by a large iron gate, with the first lodge beside it. Then you went along at a trot on a smooth road between groups of large old trees. Then came another lodge and another gate, which brought you to the house and the gardens. Past this were the home paddock, the old orchard and the stables. There was room for many horses and carriages. But I only need to tell about the stable that I was taken into. It was very large, with four good stalls. A big window that swung open looked onto the yard, which made it nice and full of fresh air.

paragraphs.context: After breakfast he came and fitted me with a bridle
paragraphs.mainIdea: John puts a bridle and a saddle on the new horse and rides him. They go slowly, then trot, canter and gallop on the common.
paragraphs.simple: After breakfast John came and put a bridle on me. He was very careful to make the straps looser or tighter so that it would fit my head well. Then he brought a saddle, but it was not wide enough for my back. He saw this at once and went for another one, which fitted well. First he rode me slowly, then at a trot, then at a canter. When we were on the common he touched me lightly with his whip, and we had a splendid gallop.

paragraphs.context: I was quite happy in my new place, and if there was one thing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Beauty is happy in his new home, but he misses his freedom. A young horse full of life finds it hard to stand in a stable all day. John is patient with him.
paragraphs.simple: I was quite happy in my new place. If there was one thing I missed, you must not think that I was not happy. Everyone who had to do with me was good, I had a light stable with plenty of fresh air, and I had the best food. What more could I want? Freedom! For three and a half years of my life I had all the freedom I could wish for. But now, week after week and month after month, and no doubt year after year, I must stand in a stable night and day, except when I am wanted. And then I must be as steady and quiet as any old horse who has worked for twenty years. There are straps here and straps there, a bit in my mouth, and blinkers over my eyes. I am not complaining, because I know it must be so. I only mean to say that it is hard for a young horse full of strength and spirit. He is used to a big field or open land, where he can throw up his head and his tail and gallop away at full speed, then turn and come back with a snort to his friends. I say it is hard never to have a little more freedom to do what you like. Sometimes, when I have had less exercise than usual, I feel so full of life and energy that I really cannot keep quiet when John takes me out to exercise. Whatever I do, it seems I must jump or dance or prance, and I know I must have given him many a good shake, especially at the start. But he was always good and patient.

paragraphs.context: There was one —the old master, Mr. Ryder —who, I think
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ginger says that old Mr. Ryder was kind, but his son Samson was hard and cruel. Samson wanted to take all the spirit out of her.
paragraphs.simple: Ginger went on: There was one man, the old master, Mr. Ryder, who she thinks could soon have brought her round and could have done anything with her. But he had given up all the hard work of the trade to his son and to another man who knew the work, and he only came now and then to watch over things. His son was a strong, tall, bold man. They called him Samson, and he liked to say that he had never found a horse that could throw him. He had no gentleness in him, as his father had. He was only hard: a hard voice, a hard eye and a hard hand. From the start, Ginger felt that he wanted to take all the spirit out of her and make her into a quiet, humble horse that did what it was told. He thought of her as nothing but horseflesh. Ginger stamped her foot as if the very thought of him made her angry.
paragraphs.main: Ginger says that old Mr. Ryder could have brought her round, but he left the hard work to his son Samson. Samson was hard, and wanted to take all the spirit out of her.

paragraphs.context: After my breaking in,” she said, “I was bought by a dealer
paragraphs.mainIdea: After breaking in, a dealer buys Ginger and sells her to a fashionable gentleman in London. There she is made to wear a checkrein that is pulled even tighter, and she hates it.
paragraphs.simple: Ginger said that after her breaking in she was bought by a dealer to make a pair with another chestnut horse. For some weeks he drove them together. Then they were sold to a gentleman who liked the newest styles, and they were sent up to London. The dealer had driven her with a checkrein, and she hated it more than anything else. But in this place they pulled the reins much tighter, because the coachman and his master thought they looked more stylish that way. They were often driven around in the park and other places where fashionable people went. Ginger says that Black Beauty, who never had a checkrein on, does not know what it is, but she can tell him that it is terrible.

paragraphs.context: Besides,” he went on, “if I took to kicking where should I be
paragraphs.mainIdea: Merrylegs says that if he began to kick he would soon be sold. He could end up with a cruel owner who works him very hard.
paragraphs.simple: Merrylegs went on: if he began to kick, where would he be? He would be sold in a very short time, and he would have no good name. He might be worked very hard by a butcher’s boy, or worked to death at some place by the sea, where no one cared about him except to find out how fast he could go. Or he might be beaten along in some cart with three or four big men in it, going out for a Sunday of noisy fun. He has often seen this in the place where he lived before he came here. He shook his head and said that he hoped he would never come to that.

paragraphs.context: I consider,” said Sir Oliver, “that blinkers are dangerous things
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sir Oliver says that blinkers are dangerous at night because horses can see better in the dark than men. He gives two examples of accidents that blinkers may have caused.
paragraphs.simple: Sir Oliver says that he thinks blinkers are dangerous things at night. Horses can see much better in the dark than men can, and many accidents would not have happened if horses had the full use of their eyes. He remembers that some years ago a hearse with two horses was coming back one dark night, by Farmer Sparrow’s house, where the pond is close to the road. The wheels went too near the edge, and the hearse fell over into the water. Both horses drowned, and the driver only just got away. After this accident they put up a strong white rail that could be seen easily. But if those horses had not been partly blind, they would have stayed further from the edge themselves, and there would have been no accident. When their master’s carriage fell over, before Black Beauty came, people said that John would have seen the big hole that the road-makers had left if the lamp on the left side had not gone out. Sir Oliver says that may be so, but if old Colin had not had blinkers on, he would have seen the hole with or without a lamp, because he was far too clever an old horse to run into danger. As it was, Colin was badly hurt and the carriage was broken, and nobody knew how John got away.

paragraphs.context: So do I,” said master, “as well as any man
paragraphs.mainIdea: The master says he likes horses to hold their heads up, but not when the head is held up by force. He says horses were meant to have their heads free, and fashion is a poor guide.
paragraphs.simple: The master says that he likes to see horses hold their heads up as much as any man does, but he does not like to see them held up. That takes away all the pleasure. He tells Langley, who is a military man, that Langley likes to see his soldiers look good on parade, with their heads up. But he would not be proud of their drill if all his men had their heads tied to a board. It might do little harm on parade, except to worry and tire them. But in a charge with bayonets against the enemy, when they need to use every muscle and push all their strength forward, he would not give much for their chance of winning. It is the same with horses. If you worry them and make them upset, you take away their power. You do not let them throw their weight against their work, so they have to do too much with their joints and muscles, and it wears them out faster. You can be sure that horses were meant to have their heads free, as free as men’s heads. If people acted a little more by common sense and a good deal less by fashion, many things would work more easily. And if a horse makes a wrong step, it has much less chance to get back on its feet if its head and neck are fastened back. The master laughs and says that he has taken his hobby out for a good trot, and asks whether the captain cannot make up his mind to get on it too, because his example would go a long way.

paragraphs.context: “You Beauty!” said John, and took the bridle
paragraphs.mainIdea: The men learn that the bridge is broken, and they are glad the horse did not go on. Master and John speak about how animals know things without reason, and how they have saved the lives of men.
paragraphs.simple: “Thank God!” said my master. “You Beauty!” said John. He took the bridle and gently turned me to the right-hand road by the river. The sun had gone down some time before. The wind seemed to have become calmer after the wild gust that tore up the tree. It grew darker and darker, and stiller and stiller. I trotted quietly along, and the wheels hardly made a sound on the soft road. For a good while neither master nor John spoke. Then master began to speak in a serious voice. I could not understand much of what they said, but I found that they thought this: if I had gone on as the master wanted, the bridge would most likely have broken under us. Then horse, chaise, master and man would have fallen into the river. The water was flowing very strongly, and there was no light and no help near, so we would more than likely all have drowned. Master said that God had given men reason, so that they could find things out for themselves. But he had given animals a kind of knowledge that does not depend on reason. It is much quicker and more perfect in its way, and by it animals have often saved the lives of men. John had many stories to tell about dogs and horses and the wonderful things they had done. He thought people did not value their animals half enough and did not make friends of them as they should. I am sure he makes friends of them if any man ever did.

paragraphs.context: So we went on, John chuckling all the way home
paragraphs.mainIdea: James tells how he once found Bill pulling the wings off flies and hit him. The master later said that cruelty is the devil’s own mark, and kindness is God’s mark.
paragraphs.simple: So they went on, with John laughing quietly all the way home. Then he told James about it. James said, “Serve him right.” James knew that boy at school. Bill was proud because he was a farmer’s son, and he would walk around in a proud way and be cruel to the small boys. The older boys did not allow that. They told him that in the school and the playground the sons of farmers and the sons of workers were all the same. One day, before school in the afternoon, James found Bill at the big window, catching flies and pulling off their wings. Bill did not see him, and James hit him on the ears so that he fell down flat on the floor. James was angry, but he was almost afraid too, because Bill roared and shouted so loudly. The boys ran in from the playground, and the master ran in from the road to see who was being killed. James told the truth at once about what he had done and why. He showed the master the flies, some crushed and some crawling about, and the wings on the window sill. James had never seen the master so angry. But Bill was still howling and crying like the coward he was, so the master did not punish him any more in that way. He put Bill on a stool for the rest of the afternoon and said that he could not go out to play for that week. Then the master spoke to all the boys in a serious way about cruelty. He said that it was hard-hearted and cowardly to hurt the weak and those who cannot help themselves. What stayed in James’s mind was this: the master said that cruelty was the devil’s own trademark. If we saw anyone who liked being cruel, we might know whom he belonged to, because the devil was a murderer from the beginning and a tormentor to the end. But where we saw people who loved their neighbors, and were kind to man and beast, we might know that this was God’s mark.

paragraphs.context: it was fully settled that James should go to Clifford Hall
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is settled that James will go to Clifford Hall in a month or six weeks, and meanwhile he gets driving practice. The carriage goes out more often, and James drives.
paragraphs.simple: A few days after this talk it was all decided that James would go to Clifford Hall in a month or six weeks, as it suited his master. In the meantime he was to get all the practice in driving that he could. I had never known the carriage to go out so often before. When the mistress did not go out, the master drove himself in the chaise with two wheels. But now, whether it was the master or the young ladies, or only a small job for someone, Ginger and I were put in the carriage and James drove us. At first John rode on the box with him and told him this and that, and after that James drove alone.

paragraphs.context: After this it was decided by my master and mistress to pay a visit
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the journey James drives carefully. He uses the brake going downhill, keeps the horses on smooth ground and gives them a rest on long hills.
paragraphs.simple: After this my master and mistress decided to pay a visit to some friends who lived about forty-six miles from our home, and James was to drive them. The first day we traveled thirty-two miles. There were some long, heavy hills, but James drove so carefully and thoughtfully that we were not troubled at all. He never forgot to put on the brake as we went downhill, or to take it off at the right place. He kept our feet on the smoothest part of the road. If the hill going up was very long, he put the wheels of the carriage a little across the road so that it would not run back, and he let us stop to get our breath. All these little things help a horse very much, especially if he gets kind words as well.

paragraphs.context: No doubt we were very foolish, but danger seemed to be all round
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horses are afraid and will not move. Smoke and a red light show the fire is near, and the old hostler comes to help.
paragraphs.simple: No doubt we were very foolish, but danger seemed to be all around, and there was nobody we knew and could trust, and everything was strange and not clear. The fresh air that came in through the open door made it easier to breathe, but the rushing sound over our heads grew louder. As I looked up through the bars of my empty rack, I saw a red light moving up and down on the wall. Then I heard a cry of “Fire!” outside, and the old hostler came in quietly and quickly. He got one horse out and went to another, but the flames were playing round the trapdoor, and the roaring overhead was terrible.
paragraphs.main: The horses are afraid, and there is nobody they know to trust. A red light shows on the wall. The old hostler comes in and gets a horse out, but the fire is near the trapdoor.

paragraphs.context: I don’t often speak of myself,” said John, “but as you are going
paragraphs.mainIdea: John tells James how he lost his parents when he was young and was helped by the mistress and by Norman, and says that is why he is glad to help little Joe.
paragraphs.simple: John says he does not often speak about himself. But as James is going away from them out into the world to manage for himself, John will tell him how he looks at these things. He was just as old as Joseph is when his father and mother died of a fever, within ten days of each other. They left him and his sister Nelly, who could not walk well, alone in the world with no relation to help them. He was a farm boy and did not earn enough to keep himself, and much less both of them. She would have had to go to the workhouse if it were not for their mistress. Nelly calls her her angel, and she is right to. The mistress got a room for Nelly with old Widow Mallet. She gave her knitting and sewing work when she could do it. When Nelly was ill she sent her dinners and many nice, comfortable things, and she was like a mother to her. Then the master took John into the stable under old Norman, who was the coachman then. John had his food at the house, a bed in the loft, a suit of clothes and three shillings a week, so he could help Nelly. Norman could have said that at his age he could not be troubled with a raw boy from the plow, but he was like a father to John and took great trouble with him. When the old man died some years later, John took his place. Now he has the best pay and can save money for a rainy day or a sunny day, and Nelly is as happy as a bird. So John is not the man to look down on a little boy and upset a good, kind master. He will miss James very much, but they will get through. He says nothing is better than doing a kindness when it comes your way, and he is glad he can do it.
paragraphs.main: John tells James how he lost his parents when he was young, and how the mistress and old Norman helped him and his sister Nelly. He says he would not look down on a little boy.

paragraphs.context: I will not tell about our way back. The doctor was a heavier
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the way back, the doctor lets the horse breathe, then Joe makes a mistake: he does not put the warm cloth on the hot horse and gives cold water. Black Beauty gets very cold and ill, and John comes and helps him.
paragraphs.simple: I will not tell about our way back. The doctor was a heavier man than John and not so good a rider, but I did my very best. The man at the tollgate had it open. When we came to the hill, the doctor stopped me. “Now, my good fellow,” he said, “take some breath.” I was glad he did, because I was nearly worn out, but that rest helped me on, and soon we were in the park. Joe was at the lodge gate, and my master was at the hall door, because he had heard us coming. He did not say a word. The doctor went into the house with him, and Joe led me to the stable. I was glad to get home. My legs shook under me, and I could only stand and breathe hard. I did not have a dry hair on my body, the water ran down my legs, and I steamed all over, like a pot on the fire, as Joe used to say. Poor Joe was young and small, and as yet he knew very little, and his father, who would have helped him, had been sent to the next village. But I am sure he did the very best he knew. He rubbed my legs and my chest, but he did not put my warm cloth on me, because he thought I was so hot that I would not like it. Then he gave me a pail of water to drink. It was cold and very good, and I drank it all. Then he gave me some hay and some corn, and thinking he had done right, he went away. Soon I began to shake and tremble, and I turned very cold. My legs ached, my loins ached and my chest ached, and I felt sore all over. How I wished for my warm, thick cloth as I stood and trembled! I wished for John, but he had eight miles to walk. So I lay down in my straw and tried to go to sleep. After a long time I heard John at the door. I gave a low moan, because I was in great pain. He was at my side in a moment, bending down by me. I could not tell him how I felt, but he seemed to know it all. He covered me up with two or three warm cloths and then ran to the house for hot water. He made me some warm gruel, which I drank, and then I think I went to sleep.
paragraphs.main: On the way back the doctor lets the horse breathe. At home Joe rubs him but does not put on the warm cloth, and gives him cold water. The horse shakes with cold and pain until John comes and helps him.

paragraphs.context: Only ignorance! only ignorance! how can you talk about only
paragraphs.mainIdea: John says that ignorance is the worst thing in the world next to wickedness. People who say "I did not know" can still do great harm, and he gives the example of Martha Mulwash.
paragraphs.simple: John says: “Only ignorance! Only ignorance! How can you talk about only ignorance? Don’t you know that it is the worst thing in the world, after wickedness? And only heaven knows which does the most harm. If people can say, ‘Oh! I did not know, I did not mean any harm,’ they think it is all right. I suppose Martha Mulwash did not mean to kill that baby when she gave it Dalby and soothing syrups. But she did kill it, and she was tried for killing someone without meaning to.”

paragraphs.context: we were quietly returning when we came to the brick-field
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joe sees a carter beating two horses that are stuck with a heavy load of bricks. The horses are working very hard and the man is cruel.
paragraphs.simple: The note was delivered, and we were riding home quietly when we came to the brick-field. Here we saw a cart heavily loaded with bricks. The wheels had stuck fast in the thick mud of some deep ruts, and the carter was shouting and beating the two horses without any pity. Joe pulled up. It was a sad sight. The two horses were pulling and fighting with all their strength to drag the cart out, but they could not move it. Sweat ran down their legs and sides, their sides were going up and down, and every muscle was pulled tight. The man pulled hard and fiercely at the head of the front horse, swore, and beat the horses in a very cruel way.

paragraphs.context: When we reached the railway station I think mistress walked from the carriage
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the station the mistress says goodbye to John. John cannot answer. The train leaves with sad people on it.
paragraphs.simple: When they reached the railway station, Black Beauty thinks the mistress walked from the carriage to the waiting-room. He heard her say in her own sweet voice, “Goodbye, John. God bless you.” He felt the rein move with a pull, but John did not answer. Maybe he could not speak. As soon as Joe had taken the things out of the carriage, John told him to stand by the horses while he went on the platform. Poor Joe stood close to the horses’ heads to hide his tears. Very soon the train came into the station with a puffing sound. Then two or three minutes later the doors were shut with a bang, the guard blew his whistle, and the train moved smoothly away. It left behind only clouds of white smoke and some very sad hearts.
paragraphs.main: At the station the mistress says goodbye to John, and John cannot answer. The train goes away and leaves sad hearts behind.

paragraphs.context: York came round to our heads and shortened the rein himself
paragraphs.mainIdea: York shortens the rein by one hole, and Black Beauty finds it hard to go uphill with his head up. Ginger says it is not so bad yet.
paragraphs.simple: York came round to the horses' heads and shortened the rein himself, by one hole, Black Beauty thinks. Every little bit makes a difference, for better or worse, and that day they had a steep hill to go up. Then Black Beauty began to understand what he had heard about. He wanted to put his head forward and pull the carriage up with all his will, as they used to do. But now he had to pull with his head up. That took all the spirit out of him, and the strain came on his back and legs. When they came in, Ginger said, “Now you see what it is like. But this is not bad. If it does not get much worse than this I shall say nothing about it, because we are very well treated here. But if they pull me up tight, they had better take care! I can’t bear it, and I won’t.”

paragraphs.context: York came to me first, while the groom stood at Ginger’s head
paragraphs.mainIdea: York pulls the rein tight. Ginger rears, kicks and falls over the carriage pole, and York sits on her head. Beauty is freed and led to his box, angry and sore.
paragraphs.simple: York came to me first, while the groom stood at Ginger’s head. He pulled my head back and fixed the rein so tight that it was almost too much to bear. Then he went to Ginger, who was jerking her head up and down against the bit without patience, as she did now. She had a good idea of what was coming. The moment York took the rein off the terret to make it shorter, she used her chance and reared up so suddenly that York’s nose was hit hard and his hat was knocked off. The groom was nearly thrown off his feet. At once they both ran to her head. But she was strong enough for them, and went on plunging, rearing and kicking in a wild way. At last she kicked right over the carriage pole and fell down, after giving me a hard blow on my near quarter. No one can know what more harm she might have done if York had not quickly sat down flat on her head to stop her struggling. At the same time he called out, “Unbuckle the black horse! Run for the winch and unscrew the carriage pole! Cut the trace here, somebody, if you can’t unhitch it!” One of the footmen ran for the winch, and another brought a knife from the house. The groom soon set me free from Ginger and the carriage and led me to my box. He just put me in as I was and ran back to York. What had happened excited me very much. If I had ever been used to kick or rear, I am sure I would have done it then. But I never had. So there I stood, angry, with a sore leg, my head still pulled up to the terret on the saddle, and no power to get it down. I was very unhappy and wanted very much to kick the first person who came near me.

paragraphs.context: He hung my rein on one of the iron spikes
paragraphs.mainIdea: A colt bumps Lizzie and a boy cracks a whip. Lizzie kicks and runs off wildly with Lady Anne. Black Auster neighs for help, and Blantyre comes running and rides after them.
paragraphs.simple: Blantyre hung my rein on one of the iron spikes and was soon out of sight among the trees. Lizzie was standing quietly at the side of the road a few steps away, with her back to me. My young mistress was sitting easily with a loose rein, softly singing a little song. I listened to my rider’s steps until they reached the house, and I heard him knock at the door. There was a field on the other side of the road, and its gate stood open. Just then some cart horses and several young colts came trotting out in a very wild way, with a boy behind them cracking a big whip. The colts were wild and playful, and one of them ran across the road and bumped into Lizzie’s back legs. I cannot say whether it was the stupid colt, or the loud cracking of the whip, or both together, but she gave a hard kick and ran off at a wild gallop. It was so sudden that Lady Anne was nearly thrown off, but she soon got her balance back. I gave a loud, high neigh for help. Again and again I neighed, hitting the ground with my foot in my hurry, and tossing my head to get the rein loose. I did not have to wait long. Blantyre came running to the gate. He looked about with worry and just saw the flying shape, now far away on the road. In a moment he jumped into the saddle. I needed no whip and no spur, because I was as eager as my rider. He saw it, and gave me a free rein, and leaned a little forward, and we raced after them.

paragraphs.context: This could not go on; no horse could keep his footing under such circumstances
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Beauty falls on both knees from pain. Smith is thrown off and does not get up. The horse stands in pain and listens for help.
paragraphs.simple: This could not go on. No horse could keep his feet under such a strain, because the pain was too great. I fell hard on both knees. Smith was thrown off by my fall, and because of my speed he must have fallen with great force. I soon got up and limped to the side of the road, where there were no stones. The moon had just come up over the hedge, and by its light I could see Smith lying a few yards from me. He did not get up. He tried a little to do so, and then there was a heavy groan. I could have groaned too, because I was in great pain in my foot and knees. But horses are used to bearing their pain without a sound, so I made no sound. I stood there and listened. I heard one more heavy groan from Smith. He now lay in full moonlight, but I could see no movement. I could do nothing for him or for myself, but how I listened for the sound of a horse, or wheels, or steps! Not many people used the road, and at that time of night we might wait for hours before help came. I stood watching and listening. It was a calm, sweet April night. There were no sounds except a few low notes of a nightingale, and nothing moved except the white clouds near the moon and a brown owl that flew quickly over the hedge. It made me think of the summer nights long ago, when I used to lie beside my mother in the green, pleasant meadow at Farmer Grey’s.

paragraphs.context: The next day after the farrier had examined my wounds, he said he hoped
paragraphs.mainIdea: The farrier hopes the joint is not hurt. The horse might still work, but would always have a mark. The cure was long and painful.
paragraphs.simple: The next day, after the farrier had looked at my wounds, he said he hoped the joint was not hurt. If it was not, I would not be spoiled for work, but I would always keep the mark. I believe they did their best to make a good cure, but it was a long and painful one. What they called proud flesh came up in my knees and was burned out with a strong chemical. When it was at last healed, they put a liquid on the front of both knees to make all the hair come off. They had some reason for this, and I think it was all right.

paragraphs.context: As soon as my knees were sufficiently healed I was turned
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Beauty is left alone in a meadow and feels lonely. Then Ginger is brought in; she has been ruined by hard riding.
paragraphs.simple: As soon as my knees were well enough, I was put in a small meadow for a month or two. No other animal was there, and although I enjoyed the freedom and the sweet grass, I had lived with other horses for so long that I felt very lonely. Ginger and I had become close friends, and now I missed her very much. I often neighed when I heard horses’ feet passing in the road, but I seldom got an answer. Then one morning the gate was opened, and who should come in but dear old Ginger! The man took off her halter and left her there. I trotted up to her with a happy whinny. We were both glad to meet, but I soon found that she was not brought to be with me for our pleasure. Her story would be too long to tell, but the end of it was that hard riding had ruined her, and she was now sent away to see what rest would do.

paragraphs.context: Besides, these drivers are often careless altogether
paragraphs.mainIdea: A careless driver lets a stone get into the horse's foot. He laughs and jokes with the lady and children, and does not look at the road or his horse.
paragraphs.simple: These drivers are also often careless altogether, and pay attention to anything else more than their horses. One day I went out in the phaeton with one of them. He had a lady and two children behind. He moved the reins about loosely as we started, and gave me several cuts with the whip for no reason, although I had already started well. There had been a lot of road-mending, and even where the stones were not freshly laid there were many loose ones about. My driver was laughing and joking with the lady and the children and talking about the country on the right and the left. But he never thought it worth the trouble to watch his horse or to drive on the smoothest parts of the road. So it easily happened that I got a stone in one of my front feet.

paragraphs.context: I well remember one spring evening I and Rory had been out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rory and Black Beauty meet a gig coming fast round a corner. The shaft of the gig runs into Rory's chest, and Rory is badly hurt.
paragraphs.simple: I remember well one spring evening when Rory and I had been out for the day. Rory was the horse that mostly went with me when a pair was asked for, and he was a good honest fellow. We had our own driver, and he was always kind and careful with us, so we had a very nice day. We were coming home at a good fast pace, about twilight. Our road turned sharp to the left. But we were close to the hedge on our own side and there was plenty of room to pass, so our driver did not pull us in. As we got near the corner, I heard a horse and two wheels coming quickly down the hill toward us. The hedge was high and I could see nothing, but the next moment we were upon each other. Luckily for me, I was on the side next to the hedge. Rory was on the left side of the pole, and he did not even have a shaft to protect him. The man driving was heading straight for the corner, and when he saw us he had no time to pull over to his own side. The whole shock came upon Rory. The shaft of the gig ran right into his chest and made him stagger back with a cry that I shall never forget. The other horse was thrown onto his back legs and one shaft was broken. It turned out that it was a horse from our own stables with the high-wheeled gig that the young men liked so much.

paragraphs.context: For a few days all went on well. I found that my groom
paragraphs.mainIdea: At first the groom does his job well, but then the horse's oats become fewer and fewer. The horse becomes weaker, but cannot complain.
paragraphs.simple: For a few days all went well. I found that my groom knew his job. He kept the stable clean and full of fresh air, and he cleaned me well, and was always gentle. He had been a hostler in one of the great hotels in Bath. He had given that up, and now he grew fruit and vegetables to sell at the market, and his wife raised poultry and rabbits and made them fat for sale. After a while it seemed to me that my oats were coming very short. I had the beans, but bran was mixed with them instead of oats, of which there were very few, certainly not more than a quarter of what there should have been. In two or three weeks this began to show in my strength and spirits. The grass food, although very good, was not enough to keep me in good shape without corn. But I could not complain or make my needs known. So it went on for about two months, and I wondered that my master did not see that something was wrong. But one afternoon he rode out into the country to see a friend of his, a gentleman farmer who lived on the road to Wells.

paragraphs.context: Alfred Smirk considered himself very handsome; he spent a great deal of time
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alfred Smirk is vain and lazy and does not clean the box. The smell and fumes make the horse's eyes sore and take away his wish to eat.
paragraphs.simple: Alfred Smirk thought he was very handsome. He spent a great deal of time on his hair, whiskers and necktie, in front of a little looking-glass in the harness-room. When his master was speaking to him, it was always, “Yes, sir; yes, sir,” and he touched his hat at every word. Everyone thought he was a very nice young man and that Mr. Barry was lucky to find him. I would say that he was the laziest man I ever came near, and the one who thought most highly of himself. Of course it was a great thing not to be treated badly, but a horse needs more than that. I had a loose box and might have been very comfortable if he had not been too lazy to clean it out. He never took all the straw away, and the smell from what lay underneath was very bad. The strong gases that rose up made my eyes sore and red, and I did not feel the same wish to eat my food.

paragraphs.context: Long strings of young horses out of the country, fresh from the marshes
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horse fair has many kinds of horses: young ones, small ponies, cart horses, and fine horses that have a fault. Some tired old horses look sad and hopeless.
paragraphs.simple: There were long lines of young horses from the country, fresh from the wet land, and groups of shaggy little Welsh ponies no taller than Merrylegs. There were hundreds of cart horses of all kinds, some with their long tails twisted up and tied with red cord. There were many like me, handsome and from a good family, but they had fallen into the middle class through some accident or fault, or weak breathing, or some other problem. Some fine animals were in their best years and fit for anything. They were throwing out their legs and showing off their paces in fine style as they were trotted out on a leading rein, with the groom running by the side. But in the background there were a number of poor horses, sadly worn out by hard work. Their knees were bending forward and their back legs were swinging out at every step. There were some very sad-looking old horses, with the lower lip hanging down and the ears lying back heavily, as if there was no more pleasure in life and no more hope. Some were so thin that you could see all their ribs, and some had old sores on their backs and hips. These were sad things for a horse to look at, who does not know whether he may come to the same state.

paragraphs.context: After driving through the side street we came to the large
paragraphs.mainIdea: The new cab horse sees the cab stand with its row of cabs, men and horses. Some of the cab men look at him and say what they think about him.
paragraphs.simple: After driving through the side street we came to the large cab stand where Jerry had said “Good night.” On one side of this wide street were tall houses with wonderful shop fronts. On the other side was an old church and churchyard, with an iron fence round it. Along this fence a number of cabs were waiting for passengers, and bits of hay were lying on the ground. Some of the men were standing together and talking, and some were sitting on their boxes reading the newspaper. One or two were feeding their horses with bits of hay and giving them a drink of water. We stopped in the line behind the last cab. Two or three men came round and began to look at me and give their opinions about me.

paragraphs.context: My master, my dear master was cheering on his comrades
paragraphs.mainIdea: Captain's master is hit by a ball in the charge, and falls from the saddle. Captain is driven away by the other riders.
paragraphs.simple: Captain says that his master, his dear master, was cheering on his friends with his right arm up in the air when one of the balls, flying close to Captain’s head, hit him. Captain felt him stagger with the shock, though he made no cry. Captain tried to slow down, but the sword fell from his master’s right hand, the rein fell loose from the left, and he sank backward from the saddle and fell to the ground. The other riders went past them, and the force of their charge drove Captain away from that place.

paragraphs.context: Just then the cart in front of us began to move on
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cart in front moves on, and Jerry and Jack get through the traffic fast. They reach the station just before twelve o'clock.
paragraphs.simple: Just then the cart in front of us began to move on, and we had a good run. We went in and out, in and out, as fast as a horse could go. Surprisingly, we had a good, clear run on London Bridge, because a whole line of cabs and carriages were all going our way at a quick trot, perhaps wanting to catch that same train. In any case, we rushed into the station with many others, just as the great clock showed eight minutes to twelve o’clock.

paragraphs.context: I should be glad to oblige the lady, sir, but I had
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jerry explains why he does not want to work on Sundays. He had a seven-day license before, but it was too hard for him and his horses. He wants Sundays for rest, with his family, and to go to church.
paragraphs.simple: Jerry says he would be glad to do a kind thing for the lady, but he had a seven-day license once, and the work was too hard for him and for his horses. It was year in and year out, not a day’s rest, and never a Sunday with his wife and children. He was never able to go to a place of worship, which he had always been used to do before he took to the driving box. So for the last five years he has only had a six-day license, and he finds it better all round.
paragraphs.main: Jerry explains why he does not want to work on Sundays. He once had a seven-day license, but it was too hard for him and his horses. He wants Sundays for rest, for his family, and for a place of worship.

paragraphs.context: Why, Polly, you are as good as the minister, and so
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jerry agrees to take Dinah in his cab, with a light trap borrowed from the butcher. He jokes that Polly is as good as the minister, and says he has had his sermon early.
paragraphs.simple: Jerry says that Polly is as good as the minister. He has had his Sunday-morning sermon early today, so she may go and tell Dinah that he will be ready for her when the clock strikes ten. But first she must go to butcher Braydon’s house with his kind words and ask if he will lend Jerry his light trap. Jerry knows that the butcher never uses it on Sunday, and it would make a great difference to the horse.
paragraphs.main: Jerry says that Polly is as good as the minister. He will be ready for Dinah at ten, and asks Polly to go and ask the butcher for his light trap.

paragraphs.context: When the streets were slippery with frost or snow
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slippery streets are the worst thing for horses. They must work hard to keep their balance, and they fear falling.
paragraphs.simple: When the streets were slippery with frost or snow, that was the worst of all for the horses. One mile of such traveling, with a weight to pull and no firm place for the feet, took more out of them than four miles on a good road. Every nerve and muscle of their bodies is under strain to keep their balance. On top of this, the fear of falling is more tiring than anything else. If the roads are very bad indeed, the horses’ shoes are roughed, but that makes them feel nervous at first.

paragraphs.context: The man flung his tattered rug over the horse, turned full round
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam says that the masters ask too much money, and the fares are too low. He and the horses must work too long, and he has no Sunday and no warm coat.
paragraphs.simple: The man threw his torn rug over the horse and turned right round to the Governor. In a voice that sounded almost hopeless he said that if the police had any business with the matter, it ought to be with the masters who charge so much, or with the fares that are fixed so low. A man has to pay eighteen shillings a day for a cab and two horses, as many of them must in the season, and he must make that money before he earns a penny for himself. Sam says that is more than hard work. He says that nine shillings a day must be got out of each horse before a man begins to get his own living. He says the Governor knows it is true. If the horses do not work, they must starve, and Sam and his children have known what that is. He has six children, and only one earns anything. He is on the stand fourteen or sixteen hours a day, and he has not had a Sunday for these ten or twelve weeks. He says that Skinner never gives a day if he can help it. He wants a warm coat and a mackintosh, but with so many to feed, how can he get them? He had to give his clock to a man for money a week ago, to pay Skinner, and he will never see it again.
paragraphs.main: Sam says that the masters charge too much and the fares are too low. He and the horses must work very long hours, and he has had no Sunday for weeks and has no warm coat.

paragraphs.context: It was Ginger! but how changed! The beautifully arched and glossy neck
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ginger is very changed. Her neck is thin and straight, her legs are swollen and her face is full of suffering. She coughs and breathes badly.
paragraphs.simple: It was Ginger! But how changed! Her neck, once beautifully curved and shiny, was now straight and thin and fallen in. Her clean, straight legs and fine lower legs were swollen. Her joints had grown out of shape with hard work. Her face, which was once so full of spirit and life, was now full of suffering. By the movement of her sides and her frequent cough, I could tell how bad her breathing was.

paragraphs.context: How many times shall I tell you not to drive in this way
paragraphs.mainIdea: The butcher is angry with his son for driving the horse too hard, and says that he has ruined a horse before. He says he must look out for himself.
paragraphs.simple: The butcher asks how many times he must tell the lad not to drive in this way. The lad ruined the last horse and broke its breathing, and he is going to ruin this one in the same way. If the lad were not his own son, the butcher would send him away at once. It is a disgrace to have a horse brought to the shop in a state like that. The lad might be taken by the police for such driving, and if he is, he need not look to his father for bail money, because the father has spoken to him until he is tired. The lad must look out for himself.

paragraphs.context: My boy, Liberty does not come from colors
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jerry tells Harry that liberty does not come from colors. A color only shows a party, and often it brings only the liberty to get drunk, abuse others and shout at an election.
paragraphs.simple: Jerry tells Harry that liberty does not come from colors. They only show which party a person is with. All the liberty a person can get out of them is the liberty to get drunk at other people’s cost, the liberty to ride to the voting place in a dirty old cab, the liberty to say bad things to anyone who does not wear your color, and the liberty to shout until your voice is rough at something you only half understand. Jerry says that is Harry’s liberty!

paragraphs.context: I found I had a good feed of crushed oats wetted
paragraphs.mainIdea: The streets are full on election day, with cabs rushing about. Many horses have a bad time, and the voters inside do not think about them.
paragraphs.simple: I found that I had a good feed of crushed oats made wet with a little bran. This would be a treat any day, but it was very refreshing then. Jerry was so thoughtful and kind. What horse would not do his best for such a master? Then he took out one of Polly’s meat pies and began to eat it, standing near me. The streets were very full, and the cabs with the candidates’ colors on them were rushing about through the crowd as if life and body were of no value. We saw two people knocked down that day, and one was a woman. The horses were having a bad time, poor things! But the voters inside did not think about that. Many of them were half-drunk and were shouting “Hurrah” out of the cab windows if their own party came by. It was the first election I had seen, and I do not want to be in another, though I have heard that things are better now.

paragraphs.context: I had hard work at it for several weeks; you see
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jerry tells Grant how he stopped drinking. It was hard work, but his wife helped him, and now for ten years he has not tasted a drop.
paragraphs.simple: Jerry says that he had hard work at it for several weeks. He never did get drunk, but he found that he was not his own master, and that when the craving came on, it was hard to say no. He saw that one of them must give way, the drink devil or Jerry Barker. He said it should not be Jerry Barker, with God’s help. It was a struggle, and he wanted all the help he could get. Until he tried to break the habit, he did not know how strong it was. But Polly took great trouble to make sure that he had good food. When the craving came, he would get a cup of coffee or some peppermint, or read a little in his book, and that helped him. Sometimes he had to say over and over to himself, “Give up the drink or lose your soul! Give up the drink or break Polly’s heart!” But thanks be to God and his dear wife, his chains were broken, and now for ten years he has not tasted a drop and never wishes for it.

paragraphs.context: The wind had been very changeable, with squalls of rain during the day
paragraphs.mainIdea: On New Year's night Jerry waits in cold sleet outside a house with no shelter. He starts to cough and sits in the cab with his feet on the pavement.
paragraphs.simple: The wind had been very changeable, with short, strong gusts of rain during the day. But now it came on sharp, driving sleet that seemed to come from all sides. It was very cold and there was no shelter. Jerry got off his box and came and pulled one of my cloths a little more over my neck. Then he walked up and down a few times, stamping his feet. Then he began to beat his arms, but that made him cough. So he opened the cab door and sat at the bottom with his feet on the pavement, and had a little shelter. The clock still rang the quarter hours, and no one came. At half-past twelve he rang the bell and asked the servant if he would be wanted that night.

paragraphs.context: Again I started the heavy load, and struggled on a few yards
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horse tries again and again to pull the load, and Jakes whips him. The horse is hurt in his mind as much as his body. Then a lady steps up and asks Jakes to stop.
paragraphs.simple: I started the heavy load again and struggled on a few yards. Again the whip came down, and again I struggled forward. The pain of that great cart whip was sharp, but my mind was hurt just as much as my poor sides. It was so hard to be punished and abused when I was doing my very best that it took the heart out of me. A third time he was beating me cruelly when a lady stepped quickly up to him and said in a sweet, serious voice, “Oh! Please do not whip your good horse any more. I am sure he is doing all he can, and the road is very steep. I am sure he is doing his best.”
paragraphs.main: The horse tries again and again to pull the load, and the carter whips him. The pain in his mind is as bad as the pain in his body. Then a lady steps up and asks the carter not to whip the horse any more.

paragraphs.context: I got along fairly till we came to Ludgate Hill
paragraphs.mainIdea: On Ludgate Hill the horse falls from the heavy load and exhaustion. He thinks he will die. The girl says it is their fault, and people loosen his harness and give him cordial.
paragraphs.simple: I got along fairly well until we came to Ludgate Hill. But there the heavy load and my own tiredness were too much. I was struggling to keep on, pushed forward by constant pulls on the rein and use of the whip, when in a single moment my feet slipped from under me. I cannot tell how it happened. I fell heavily to the ground on my side. The suddenness and the force with which I fell seemed to beat all the breath out of my body. I lay perfectly still. I had no power to move, and I thought I was going to die. I heard a kind of confusion round me, with loud, angry voices and the getting down of the luggage, but it was all like a dream. I thought I heard that sweet, sad voice saying, “Oh! That poor horse! It is all our fault.” Someone came and loosened the throat strap of my bridle and undid the traces which kept the collar so tight on me. Someone said, “He’s dead, he’ll never get up again.” Then I could hear a policeman giving orders, but I did not even open my eyes. I could only draw a gasping breath now and then. Some cold water was thrown over my head and some cordial was poured into my mouth, and something was covered over me. I cannot tell how long I lay there, but I found my life coming back, and a man with a kind voice was patting me and encouraging me to rise. After I had been given some more cordial, and after one or two attempts, I staggered to my feet, and was gently led to some stables close by. Here I was put into a stall with plenty of straw, and some warm gruel was brought to me, which I drank thankfully.
paragraphs.main: On Ludgate Hill the horse falls from the heavy load and from tiredness. He thinks he will die. He hears a sad voice say it is all their fault. People loosen his harness and give him cordial.

paragraphs.context: The buyers and sellers, too, many of them, looked not much better off
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the sale, the buyers and sellers are poor too. Some look hard from hard times, others are kind. A man with a boy comes to the horse and looks at him with pity.
paragraphs.simple: The buyers and sellers, many of them, did not look much better off than the poor animals they were bargaining about. There were poor old men trying to get a horse or a pony for a few pounds, to pull some little wood or coal cart. There were poor men trying to sell a worn-out horse for two or three pounds, rather than have the greater loss of killing him. Some of them looked as if poverty and hard times had made them hard all over. But there were others for whom I would gladly have used the last of my strength. They were poor and shabby, but kind and human, with voices that I could trust. One old man who walked in a shaky way liked me very much, and I liked him, but I was not strong enough. It was an anxious time! Coming from the better part of the fair, I noticed a man who looked like a gentleman farmer, with a young boy by his side. He had a broad back and round shoulders and a kind, red face, and he wore a hat with a wide edge. When he came up to me and my companions, he stood still and gave a look full of pity round at us. I saw his eye rest on me. I still had a good mane and tail, which did something for how I looked. I raised my ears and looked at him.

paragraphs.context: White star in the forehead, one white foot on the off side
paragraphs.mainIdea: The groom checks the horse's marks: the white star, the white foot, the knot in the neck and the white patch on the back. He knows it is Black Beauty and says that he is Joe Green.
paragraphs.simple: The groom says out loud: a white star on the forehead, one white foot on the off side, and this little knot in just that place. Then, looking at the middle of the horse’s back, he says that there is the little patch of white hair that John used to call “Beauty’s threepenny bit.” He says it must be Black Beauty. He asks, “Beauty, do you know me? I am little Joe Green, who almost killed you.” And he began to pat and pat the horse as if he was very happy.

paragraphs.context: pony is like a steam-engine or a thrashing-machine, and can
paragraphs.mainIdea: Merrylegs says boys think a pony is a machine that never gets tired. He threw them off so they would stop hitting him.
paragraphs.simple: Merrylegs says he is very careful with the young ladies. When they are afraid he goes quietly, and when they are fine he goes a little faster so they get used to it. He says boys are different and must be taught, as young horses are taught. After the other children had ridden him, the boys rode him for an hour and hit him with big sticks. He took it calmly until he had had enough, and he stopped as a hint. Boys think a pony is like a steam engine or a farm machine, and can go on as long as they like. They never think he can get tired or feel pain. So he rose on his hind legs and let the boy slip off. He did it to each boy until they understood. He likes the boys and says they are not cruel, but he had to teach them. James was angry when he saw the big sticks, and said sticks like that were not for young gentlemen.

paragraphs.context: a horse was something like a steam-engine, only smaller
paragraphs.mainIdea: Some drivers think a horse is a small machine. They make him keep going, however hard the road is.
paragraphs.simple: They thought a horse was like a small steam engine. If they had paid, they believed he must go as far and as fast as they wanted, and pull as heavy a load as they wanted. It did not matter if the road was heavy and wet, or dry, or stony, or smooth, or up a hill or down a hill. He had to go on and on at the same speed, with no rest and with no one thinking of him.

paragraphs.context: Come, father and mother, And sister and brother
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jerry's little song asks the whole family to come and help one another.
paragraphs.simple: The song calls the father, the mother, the sister, and the brother. It asks every one of them to come and help the others.

paragraphs.context: If you in the morning Throw minutes away
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jerry's song says that minutes wasted in the morning are gone forever.
paragraphs.simple: If you waste minutes in the morning, you cannot pick them up later in the day. You may rush and worry, but those minutes are lost forever.

sentences.context: nor the second, but it shall be the last
sentences.simple: This is not the first time, and it is not the second time, but it will be the last.
sentences.grammar: 'nor the second' carries on the negative ('not the first, nor the second'); 'shall' is the master's firm promise, not just the future.

sentences.context: I never yet could make out why men are so fond of this sport
sentences.simple: Up to now I have never been able to understand why men like this sport so much.
sentences.grammar: 'never yet could' means 'up to now I have never been able to'; 'make out' means 'understand'; 'so fond of' means 'like very much'.

sentences.context: Those who have never had a bit in their mouths
sentences.simple: Those who have never had a bit in their mouths cannot imagine how bad it feels.
sentences.grammar: 'Those who...' means 'the ones who...' (here, horses); 'cannot think how bad it feels' means 'cannot imagine' and 'how bad' starts an indirect question.

sentences.context: I never was in a better box than that
sentences.simple: That was the best box I was ever in.
sentences.grammar: 'never ... a better box than that' says it was the best box he was ever in; 'was in' is the simple past of 'to be in'.

sentences.context: If it was not for bringing back the past
sentences.simple: If it were not for bringing back the past.
sentences.grammar: 'If it was not for X, I should have...' means 'Without X, I would have...'; 'should have named' is the same as 'would have named'.

sentences.context: Spirited horses, when not enough exercised, are often called skittish
sentences.simple: Lively horses that do not get enough exercise are often called skittish, when really they are only playing.
sentences.grammar: 'when not enough exercised' is a short form of 'when they are not exercised enough'; the last 'when' means 'while in fact'.

sentences.context: he had only just mounted me on the training ground
sentences.simple: He had only just got up on my back on the training ground.
sentences.grammar: 'had only just mounted' is the past perfect: the mounting happened right before another past event (something I did put him out of temper).

sentences.context: Did not your master take any thought for you
sentences.simple: Did your master not think about you at all?
sentences.grammar: This question puts 'not' after 'Did' and before the subject, which is an old way of saying 'Didn't your master...'.

sentences.context: I would not do such a thing for the best oats
sentences.simple: I would not do such a thing for the very best oats that ever came into the stable.
sentences.grammar: 'would not do ... for the best oats' uses 'would' for a made-up case; 'that ever came' uses 'ever' to stress 'the best of all time'.

sentences.context: if the lamp on the left side had not gone out
sentences.simple: If the lamp on the left side had not gone out, John would have seen the great hole.
sentences.grammar: 'if ... had not gone out, John would have seen' is the third conditional: it talks about something in the past that did not happen.

sentences.context: if a horse makes a false step, he has much less chance
sentences.simple: If a horse takes a wrong step, he has much less chance to get his balance back.
sentences.grammar: 'recovering himself' uses the reflexive 'himself' after the -ing form to mean 'getting back his balance'; 'of' links 'chance' to the action.

sentences.context: it would be rather awkward if one of these branches came down upon us
sentences.simple: It would be rather awkward if one of these branches came down on us.
sentences.grammar: 'would be ... if one of these branches came' is a second-type 'if' sentence: it talks about something that might happen, using the past tense after 'if'.

sentences.context: I love horses, and it riles me to see them badly used
sentences.simple: I love horses, and it makes me angry to see them treated badly.
sentences.grammar: 'it riles me to see them badly used' puts 'it' first for the real subject, 'to see them badly used'; 'used' here is a past participle meaning 'treated'.

sentences.context: I would rather have them in charge with him than with half
sentences.simple: I would prefer to leave the horses with him than with half the young men I know.
sentences.grammar: 'would rather ... than ...' says what someone prefers; here 'in charge with him' means he has the care of them.

sentences.context: I never was cleaned so lightly and quickly as by that little old man
sentences.simple: No one ever cleaned me so lightly and so quickly as that little old man did.
sentences.grammar: 'never ... so lightly and quickly as ...' compares two things as equal in the negative; 'was cleaned' is the passive, with 'by that little old man' naming who did it.

sentences.context: had she not heard me outside she would never have had courage
sentences.simple: If she had not heard me outside, she would never have had the courage to come out.
sentences.grammar: 'had she not heard' is the same as 'if she had not heard'; 'if' is left out and the helping verb 'had' is put first.

sentences.context: she must have gone to the workhouse but for our mistress
sentences.simple: She would have had to go to the workhouse if it had not been for our mistress.
sentences.grammar: 'must have gone' here means 'would certainly have gone'; 'but for our mistress' means 'if it had not been for our mistress'.

sentences.context: if we had been a little longer it would have been too late
sentences.simple: If we had taken a little more time, it would have been too late.
sentences.grammar: 'if we had been ... it would have been' is the third conditional: it talks about something in the past that did not happen.

sentences.context: Don’t you know that it is the worst thing in the world
sentences.simple: Do you not know that it is the worst thing in the world, after wickedness?
sentences.grammar: A negative question, 'Don’t you know...?', is used to say strongly that the person does know; 'next to' here means 'after'.

sentences.context: Many folks would have ridden by and said it was not their business
sentences.simple: Many people would have ridden past and said it was not their job to get involved.
sentences.grammar: 'would have ridden by and said' is the third conditional: it tells what many people would have done in the past, but Joe did not.

sentences.context: Many young animals are frightened and spoiled by wrong treatment
sentences.simple: Many young animals are scared and made bad by wrong treatment.
sentences.grammar: 'frightened and spoiled' are two past participles used as passive verbs with 'are', and 'by wrong treatment' says what causes it.

sentences.context: if she were ill-used or unfairly treated she would not be unlikely
sentences.simple: If she were treated badly or unfairly, she would quite likely pay people back in the same way.
sentences.grammar: 'would not be unlikely' uses two negatives to say 'it is quite likely'; 'if she were' is the second conditional.

sentences.context: had not York promptly sat himself down flat on her head
sentences.simple: There is no knowing what more harm she might have done if York had not quickly sat down flat on her head.
sentences.grammar: 'had not York ... sat' puts 'had' before the subject to mean 'if York had not sat'; 'might have done' tells about a possible result in the past.

sentences.context: I needed no whip, no spur, for I was as eager as my rider
sentences.simple: I did not need a whip or a spur, because I wanted to go as much as my rider did.
sentences.grammar: 'as eager as my rider' compares two things that are equal with 'as ... as'; 'no whip, no spur' uses 'no' twice to stress that neither was needed.

sentences.context: If Smith had been in his right senses he would have been sensible
sentences.simple: If Smith had been thinking clearly, he would have known that something was wrong with my pace.
sentences.grammar: 'in his right senses' means 'thinking clearly'; 'sensible of' means 'aware of'; the 'if ... had been ... would have been' form is the third conditional.

sentences.context: if he had been in his right senses he would just as soon
sentences.simple: If he had been thinking clearly, he would just as soon have tried to ride him over the moon.
sentences.grammar: 'would just as soon have tried' means 'would as willingly have tried' (here, not at all); it is a third conditional with a joke.

sentences.context: The mare shall have a twelvemonth’s run, and we shall see
sentences.simple: The mare will have a year in the field, and we will see what that will do for her.
sentences.grammar: 'shall' with 'the mare' and 'we' shows the earl's decision, not just the future; 'twelvemonth’s run' is a year of free time in a field.

sentences.context: a practiced hand would have felt by the rein that there was something
sentences.simple: A driver who knew his job would have felt through the rein that something was wrong with the horse's step.
sentences.grammar: 'would have felt' is the third conditional result: it says what a good driver would have done, but this driver did not.

sentences.context: I wish I could have done so; I would have had long legs then
sentences.simple: I wish I had made myself, because then I would have had long legs.
sentences.grammar: 'I wish I could have done so' is about a past that cannot change, and 'I would have had' is the result of that unreal wish.

sentences.context: I think if he would have let me just look at things quietly
sentences.simple: I think that if he had let me just look at things quietly and see that there was nothing to hurt me, it would have been all right, and I would have got used to them.
sentences.grammar: 'if he would have let me' is a spoken way of saying 'if he had let me'; the result is 'it would have been all right'.

sentences.context: I am much mistaken if your horse gets it
sentences.simple: I would be very surprised if your horse gets it.
sentences.grammar: 'I am much mistaken if' is a polite old way to say that you are sure about something: here he is sure the horse does not get the corn.

sentences.context: I should not like to do him an injury, but I’ll do it
sentences.simple: I would not want to hurt him, but I will do it if you want me to, sir.
sentences.grammar: 'if you please' is a polite, old way to say 'if you want me to'; 'I should not like' is the same as 'I would not like'.

sentences.context: if a horse may speak his mind so far as he understands
sentences.simple: If a horse can say what he thinks, as far as he understands.
sentences.grammar: 'may speak his mind' uses 'may' to mean 'is allowed to'; 'speak his mind' means 'say what he thinks'; 'so far as' means 'as far as'.

sentences.context: I suppose I need not find it out till it finds me out
sentences.simple: I think I do not have to find out about something wrong until it shows itself.
sentences.grammar: 'it finds me out' turns the sentence round, so that the fault, not the man, is the one that finds; 'need not' means 'do not have to'.

sentences.context: I believe so long as we felt our rider firm in the saddle
sentences.simple: I believe that as long as we felt our rider was steady in the saddle, none of us gave way to fear.
sentences.grammar: 'so long as' means 'as long as'; it begins a clause that gives the condition under which none of the horses gave way to fear.

sentences.context: It’s against his conscience to go beyond a jog-trot
sentences.simple: He feels that it is wrong to go faster than a slow trot.
sentences.grammar: 'It’s against his conscience' means 'his sense of right and wrong does not let him'; it is Larry's joke about Jerry.

sentences.context: I would not have you a seven-days’ cabman again
sentences.simple: I would not want you to be a seven-day cab driver again.
sentences.grammar: 'would not have you a seven-days’ cabman' is an older pattern: 'have' with a person and a noun means 'want or allow you to be'.

sentences.context: we should do to other people as we should like
sentences.simple: We should do to other people what we would like them to do to us.
sentences.grammar: 'as we should like they should do' is an old way to say 'what we would like them to do'; it is the Golden Rule from the chapter title.

sentences.context: Do you know why this world is as bad as it is
sentences.simple: Do you know the reason this world is as bad as it is?
sentences.grammar: 'as bad as it is' means 'as bad as it now is'; 'why' starts an indirect question after 'know'.

sentences.context: I wish some of ’em had got to sit on my box
sentences.simple: I wish some of them had to sit on my box sixteen hours a day.
sentences.grammar: 'wish some of them had got to sit' uses the past tense after 'wish' for something that is not true now; 'had got to' means 'had to'.

sentences.context: I wish I may drop down dead at my work, and not be sent
sentences.simple: I hope that I will fall down dead while I work, and not be sent away to be killed.
sentences.grammar: 'I wish I may' is an older way to say 'I hope that I will'; it is followed by two actions joined with 'and not'.

sentences.context: If you were not my own son I would dismiss you on the spot
sentences.simple: If you were not my own son, I would send you away from your job right now.
sentences.grammar: 'If you were not ... I would dismiss' is the second conditional: it says what would happen if something that is not true were true; 'on the spot' means 'at once'.

sentences.context: I could not in my conscience send him up to make
sentences.simple: I could not, with a clear sense of what is right, send him up to make laws.
sentences.grammar: 'in my conscience' means 'with my sense of right and wrong'; 'send him up' means to choose him for the job of making the laws.

sentences.context: I’d be ashamed of myself to let a woman and a sick child
sentences.simple: I would feel shame if I let a woman and a sick child take a risk like that.
sentences.grammar: 'I’d be ashamed ... to let' uses 'would be' for an imagined case; 'run a risk' means 'take a chance of something bad happening'.

sentences.context: it was an ill wind that blew nobody good
sentences.simple: It was a bad wind that blew good to nobody.
sentences.grammar: 'it was an ill wind that blew nobody good' is a well-known saying: a bad event for one person often gives good luck to another; here it points to the cabman's gain.

sentences.context: if ever he gave up the cab work she would like to know
sentences.simple: She told father that if he ever stopped doing cab work, she would like to hear about it.
sentences.grammar: 'if ever he gave up' joins 'if' with 'ever' to mean 'if at any time'; 'she would like to know' is what she said to Jerry in the past.

sentences.context: Is it not better,” she said, “to lead a good fashion
sentences.simple: Is it not better to start a good fashion than to follow a bad one?
sentences.grammar: 'Is it not better...?' is a question that expects the answer 'yes'; 'one' stands for 'fashion' so the word is not said twice.

sentences.context: I wished I might, like Ginger, drop down dead at my work
sentences.simple: I wished that I could drop down dead at my work, as Ginger did, and be free from my sadness.
sentences.grammar: 'wished I might' uses 'might' for a hope; 'like Ginger' compares him with Ginger; 'be out of my misery' means 'be free from my pain'.

sentences.context: I’ll be bound he’d be worth twenty pounds next spring
sentences.simple: I am sure he will be worth twenty pounds next spring.
sentences.grammar: 'I’ll be bound' means 'I am sure'; 'he’d be worth' is 'he would be worth', and it is a guess about next spring.

sentences.context: it won’t be my fault if you haven’t good times of it now
sentences.simple: If you do not have good times now, it will not be because of me.
sentences.grammar: 'it won’t be my fault if' uses the present tense after 'if' for the future; 'good times of it' is a spoken way to say 'a good life'.

pull up.meaning: To stop a horse by pulling on the long bands.

give up.meaning: To stop doing something, or to let someone else have it.
give up.example: he had given up all the hard part of the trade

serve him right.meaning: Used to say that the bad thing that happens to someone is fair.
